newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Solana set to push Primakov on NATO-Russia ties.
newsitem.headline: Solana set to push Primakov on NATO-Russia ties.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana is expected to move on to the offensive at a second round of talks with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov later on Sunday over a new NATO-Russia relationship.

After weeks of allied concessions designed to win Moscow's approval for NATO's plans to expand eastwards, Solana will try and focus the talks on what Russia can bring to plans to set up some form of permanent consultative mechanism.

"Solana will push Primakov. What will Russia bring to a new relationship?," said one senior diplomat, adding Solana would try and focus the discussions on the content of any final document rather than the exact form it should take.
Russia wants a legally-binding treaty while NATO prefers a more flexible political agreement which would not need ratifying by member states' parliaments.

Last week, President Boris Yeltsin pushed the issue in a 15- minute telephone conversation with German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel and later in talks with the new U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.

Moscow wants the final document to contain a commitment by the allies not to place troops and weapons on the territory of new members unless they are there for internationally-approved peace-keeping operations.

NATO, committed to opposing any form of second-class membership, cannot accept outside conditions on where it positions its "infrastructure". At the same time several allies want more details of what its own military is planning.

Diplomats say Italy and France have suggested NATO examine options between a legal treaty and a political document, suggesting it may be possible to have a politically-binding agreement endorsed by governments.
"The Helsinki Final Document was not legally binding, but no one questioned its validity," said another senior diplomatic source.

Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said Russia's legitimate concerns should be taken into account and the 16 NATO allies had to make the maximum effort to make sure a deal was struck before enlargement starts next July.
"What is important is that we create a binding document on consultation," he told reporters in Brussels on Friday in the wings of an international conference on European security.
He added he could not imagine enlargement taking place without a deal with Russia although the alliance position is that it will go ahead come what may.
"We will cross that bridge when we get to it, at the moment I will not consider that we do not get a deal (with Russia)," Dini told reporters.

Italy has been angered by suggestions the issue could be resolved at a 'big power' summit of the United States, Russia, France, Britain, and Germany -- a proposal that also horrifies countries such as Poland, wary of once again being 'sold out' by the West.
Alliance sources say Solana is also likely to tell Primakov NATO has no objections to an earlier special NATO-Russia summit to formalise the agreement if that is more to Moscow's liking.
NATO, with Moscow's backing, has imposed a total news blackout on the meeting which authoritative sources say will take place over dinner at Solana's Brussels residence.
The meeting, a follow-up to one last month, follows a week of intensive diplomacy.
On the surface, there has been no progress towards removing Moscow's determined opposition to enlargement -- an issue which unites Russia's entire political class.
Mikhail Gorbachev, the last leader of the Soviet Union, warned again on Saturday that enlargement would backfire on the West by strengthening the position of anti-reform nationalist forces.
"Instead of increasing security, NATO expansion would cause an increase in threats and not only in Europe," he wrote in an article in the Italian daily La Stampa.

But behind Moscow's strident public rhetoric, alliance diplomats say there has been an acceptance they cannot stop some form of limited enlargement and are about to enter into a real dialogue on an overall NATO-Russia deal.
NATO intends to invite new members into the alliance at a summit in Madrid in July. At the same summit, they would like to endorse the new NATO-Russia charter.
NATO says enlargement -- led by Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic -- will take place whatever happens.
"Not to enlarge is the do-nothing, achieve-nothing option. It is the option the alliance long ago rejected," Solana told a conference on European security in Brussels on Friday.
